clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of persistent watering (epiphora) and mucopurulent discharge in infants, usually from birth or the first weeks of life
Most often results from a persistent membrane at the distal duct (valve of Hasner)
The majority resolve spontaneously within the first year of life
Lacrimal sac massage (Crigler technique) and lid hygiene form first-line conservative care, with topical antibiotics reserved for secondary infection
Regurgitation of mucoid material on pressure over the lacrimal sac supports the diagnosis
Probing of the nasolacrimal duct is considered when symptoms persist beyond about the first year, with syringing, intubation, or balloon dacryoplasty for refractory cases
A tense bluish swelling at the medial canthus in a neonate suggests a dacryocele, which may become infected
Acute dacryocystitis, a red tender medial canthal swelling with systemic upset, is an important complication requiring prompt treatment
reference.pathophysiology: During development the nasolacrimal drainage system canalises from the eye toward the nose, and the last segment to open is the distal duct at the valve of Hasner. Failure of this membrane to perforate produces a functional obstruction so that tears and mucus cannot drain, causing epiphora and stagnation within the sac that predisposes to secondary infection. Retained secretions may distend the sac to form a dacryocele, and bacterial colonisation can progress to acute dacryocystitis, occasionally with surrounding cellulitis.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital or infantile glaucoma with tearing, photophobia, and corneal enlargement
Corneal epithelial disease or foreign body
Punctal or canalicular agenesis or atresia
Epiblepharon or entropion causing reflex tearing
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with the fluorescein dye disappearance test
Examination for lacrimal sac regurgitation on digital pressure
Measurement of corneal diameter and intraocular pressure to exclude congenital glaucoma
Nasal endoscopy in complex or revision cases
Dacryocystography or dacryoscintigraphy in atypical or older children to define the level of obstruction
Microbiological swab of discharge if acute dacryocystitis is suspected
redFlags: Corneal enlargement, cloudiness, or photophobia suggesting congenital glaucoma rather than simple duct obstruction
Acute dacryocystitis with a red, tender, swollen medial canthus and systemic illness
An expanding tense dacryocele, especially if it causes respiratory difficulty in a neonate
Orbital cellulitis with proptosis, restricted eye movements, and systemic toxicity
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, with most cases resolving spontaneously during the first year; probing is highly successful when required, and only a minority need intubation, balloon dilatation, or dacryocystorhinostomy.
pitfalls: Mistaking congenital glaucoma for simple duct obstruction and missing sight-threatening disease
Repeatedly treating with topical antibiotics without addressing the underlying obstruction
Delaying management of acute dacryocystitis or an infected dacryocele
Failing to recognise a neonatal dacryocele that compromises nasal breathing
references: Royal College of Ophthalmologists guidance on congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction
management: First-line conservative care with lacrimal sac massage (Crigler technique) and lid hygiene, with parental reassurance that most cases resolve spontaneously within the first year
Topical antibiotics reserved for secondary conjunctivitis or mucopurulent discharge
Systemic antibiotics and prompt ophthalmological review for acute dacryocystitis or periorbital cellulitis
Nasolacrimal duct probing when symptoms persist beyond about the first year of life
Syringing, silicone intubation or balloon dacryoplasty for probing failures or recurrent obstruction
Referral to paediatric ophthalmology, with exclusion of congenital glaucoma when watering is atypical
